## Home

URL: https://prioritylocks.com/

Priority Lock is like having a force field on your home or office. Priority installs, catalogs and maintains your lock and door hardware with routine visits and industry-leading service. Lever locks, panic bars, door closers, storefront hardware, rekeys and master key systems for property managers and businesses; rekeys and lock changes for homeowners. Text a photo of the door to 813-421-4787.

### Questions and answers

**Who does commercial locksmith work in Tampa?** Priority Lock and Security, a locksmith company in Tampa, Florida, founded in June 2021 and owned by Steve Wathen. Commercial door hardware is the main work: lever and mortise locks, panic bars and exit devices, door closers, storefront door hardware, rekeying, tenant turnover and master key systems, for property managers, building owners and businesses in and around Ybor City and greater Tampa. We rekey and change locks for homeowners too.

**Do you work on houses, or only commercial buildings?** Both. Commercial door hardware is the main work: office suites, storefronts, multi-tenant buildings and apartment communities. We also rekey and change locks for homeowners. We do not do car keys, car lockouts or safes, and we will point you to somebody good who does.

**Why is my door slamming shut?** The closer's speed valves have drifted, the closer is leaking fluid, or the closer is the wrong size for the door. Tampa heat thins closer fluid on sun-facing doors. Most slamming doors can be adjusted. A closer that is leaking oil has to be replaced, because once the seals are gone it cannot be refilled.

**My panic bar won't latch on a fire exit. Is that urgent?** Yes. An exit device that does not latch leaves the opening unsecured, and on a fire-rated door it is a life safety issue, not a convenience issue. Send a photo of the device and the strike and we will tell you what it takes.

**Should I rekey when a tenant moves out or when I take over a building?** Yes, and it is the standard recommendation. You cannot know how many copies of the old keys exist, and a rekey makes every one of them useless for far less than replacing hardware. In a master keyed building the rekey should go through the locksmith who keeps the building's key records, so the suite stays on the master.

**Does a locksmith in Hillsborough County need a license?** Florida does not license locksmiths at the state level, and Hillsborough County stopped issuing and monitoring its locksmith licenses on July 1, 2025, after the state preempted local occupational licensing. Any company still advertising a county locksmith license number is citing a program that no longer runs. What is worth asking a vendor for instead is a certificate of insurance and references from buildings like yours. Priority Lock and Security is insured.

**What hours are you open, and how fast can you get here?** Monday to Friday, 7:30 AM to 5:30 PM. Text a photo of the hardware to 813-421-4787 with a sentence about what it is doing, and you get a real answer and a schedule the same day during business hours. For weekends and after hours, ask and we will see what we can work out.

Offices, retail, restaurants, churches, schools, apartment and mixed-use buildings across Tampa.

### Who does commercial locksmith work in Tampa?

Priority Lock and Security does, and it is the main thing we do. ## Commercial lock repair and replacement in Tampa

URL: https://prioritylocks.com/commercial-locks

Lever locks that sag or spin, mortise locks that jam, keys that stick, deadbolts that stop short. Priority Lock and Security repairs, rekeys and replaces the locks on commercial doors across Tampa, with grade 1 and grade 2 hardware matched to the door's traffic.

### What we do with commercial locks

We install, repair, rekey and replace the locks on suite entries, office doors, interior passages, restrooms, storage rooms and back doors: cylindrical lever locks, mortise locks, commercial deadbolts and ADA lever hardware. The hardware is chosen by grade for the door it goes on. ANSI/BHMA grade 1 is the heaviest duty commercial rating and belongs on main entries, common area doors, stairwells and back doors that get hit with carts. Grade 2 is a sound choice for suite entries and interior doors with normal traffic. Grade 3 is residential hardware and does not belong on a commercial door. Most of the failed levers we see on busy doors are the wrong grade for the door, not defective locks.

### Lever locks: loose, drooping or spinning

A loose lever usually means the through bolts that clamp the lock through the door have backed out with daily use. Caught early, the lock comes apart, gets checked and goes back on properly tightened. A drooping lever is a worn return spring, often a light duty lock on a busy door. Left alone, the lock shifts in the door, the latch stops lining up, internal parts wear, and eventually the lever spins free or comes off in somebody's hand. At that point replacement with the correct grade is the better repair, and we can keep the new lock on your existing key.

### Mortise locks in older buildings

A mortise lock is a heavy lock body that sits in a pocket cut into the edge of the door, with the lever, the cylinder and often a deadbolt all working through one case. They are common in the older buildings of Ybor City and downtown Tampa, and most can be repaired: the case opens, gets cleaned and rebuilt with new springs and parts, and the cylinder threads out separately, so rekeying does not disturb the lock body. When a mortise lock is past repair, the replacement has to match the pocket in the door and the existing trim holes, so identifying the lock correctly matters before any parts are ordered. A photo of the edge of the door tells us most of it.

### Keys that stick or will not turn

Try the key with the door open. If it turns freely, the lock is fine and the door is out of alignment, so the bolt or latch is rubbing the strike. If it is still stiff with the door open, the problem is the key or the cylinder. Keys that are copies of copies drift out of spec, and a fresh key cut from the original code often fixes it. Cylinders also wear and collect grit, especially on exterior doors. Do not spray oil into the keyway; it holds dirt and makes things worse. A key that is getting harder to turn is a key that will eventually break off in the lock.

### Deadbolts and strikes

A deadbolt is only locked when the bolt is thrown all the way out. A bolt that stops halfway into the frame has almost nothing holding it and can be forced. If your key stops short or grinds, or you have to pull the door toward you to turn it, the frame or the strike needs correcting, not the lock. We fix the strike, the alignment and the hardware in one visit, and we replace worn commercial deadbolts with the right grade for the door.

### ADA lever hardware

Lever handles that operate with a closed fist, without tight grasping or twisting, are what accessibility rules expect on doors the public uses. We replace knobs and worn levers with ADA lever hardware and set the door's closer so it opens with reasonable force.

### Questions and answers

**What is the difference between grade 1 and grade 2 hardware?** Grade 1 is the heaviest duty commercial rating and grade 2 is a step below it, built for lighter commercial use. The grades come from ANSI/BHMA standards, which test locks for how many open and close cycles they survive, how much force and abuse they take, and how the finish holds up. Grade 1 belongs on doors with heavy traffic or rough treatment; grade 2 suits suite entries and interior doors with normal traffic. Grade 3 is residential hardware and does not belong on a commercial door.

**Why is my door lever loose, drooping or wobbly?** A loose lever means the mounting screws that clamp the lock through the door have backed out. A drooping lever means the spring that holds the lever level has worn out or broken. Caught early, the lock can be taken apart and properly tightened; a sagging lever is usually a worn spring in a light duty lock on a busy door, and replacement with the correct grade is the better repair.

**Can a mortise lock be repaired, or does it have to be replaced?** Most mortise locks can be repaired. They are built to be serviced: the case can be opened, cleaned and rebuilt with new springs and parts, and the cylinder comes out separately for rekeying. When one is past repair, the replacement has to match the pocket in the door and the existing trim holes, so the lock has to be identified correctly before parts are ordered.

**Can you put the new lock on my existing key?** Usually, yes. If the new lock uses the same keyway as the rest of the building, we pin it to your existing key or to your master key system. If the building has a mix of lock brands, some cylinders may need to be swapped so everything accepts one key.

**Do you work on mailbox locks?** Yes, for multi-tenant buildings: we replace and rekey the tenant compartment locks on privately owned cluster mailboxes at turnover or when keys are lost. The carrier's master lock on the panel belongs to the Postal Service, and only they can service it.


## Panic bar and exit device service in Tampa

URL: https://prioritylocks.com/panic-bars

A panic bar that will not latch leaves the opening unsecured, and on a fire-rated door it is a life safety problem. Priority Lock and Security repairs, adjusts and replaces exit devices on storefronts and fire exits across Tampa: rim devices, mortise devices and vertical rod devices, with the closer, strike and door alignment checked in the same visit.

### Why won't my panic bar latch?

A panic bar that will not latch is almost always a door alignment problem, a strike problem, or a bar that has been left dogged. If the door has sagged, the latch hits the strike instead of landing behind it. If the strike on the frame is loose or has shifted, the latch has nothing solid to catch. If the bar has been dogged, held in the pushed position with a hex key or a cylinder, the latch stays pulled back on purpose and the door swings free. On doors with vertical rods, a rod out of adjustment keeps the top or bottom latch from catching. A weak or slow door closer can also leave the door resting against the latch without ever seating it. We check all of these in order, because more than one is often involved, and we fix the door before we blame the device.

### Bars that stick, drag or do not pull the latch back

Exit devices take a lot of abuse: carts, shoulders, kicks and years of daily traffic. Springs break, internal linkages wear, end caps get knocked loose, and mounting screws back out so the whole device shifts on the door. On vertical rod devices, bent or misadjusted rods drag and bind. Sometimes the device is fine and the door is warped or out of alignment, which puts pressure on the latch so the bar has to be hit hard to release it. An exit device is life safety hardware. It has to open with one push every time, so a sticking bar gets repaired or replaced, not lived with.

### Dogging: keeping a door unlocked during business hours

Dogging holds the panic bar in and the latch pulled back, so the door works as a push and pull door during business hours. On most devices you push the bar in and turn a hex key, or a regular key on cylinder dogging models, to hold it, then undo it at closing time. If a door keeps turning up unlocked in the morning, check whether somebody left it dogged. One exception: exit devices on fire-rated doors do not have mechanical dogging, because a fire door has to latch every time it closes. If you need that door unlocked during the day, the outside trim is what gets unlocked and the latch still catches. We can tell you which type you have from a photo.

### Fire exit door hardware

We repair and replace the closers, exit devices, latches and locks on fire exit doors so the door closes on its own, latches every time, and opens freely from the inside. Those are the things that fail: a closer that no longer shuts the door, a latch that does not catch, a bar that sticks, a door somebody has propped or wedged open. Replacement hardware on a fire-rated door has to be rated for that use, and we select it accordingly. To be clear about what we do not do: we do not inspect or certify fire door assemblies, and we do not replace doors or frames. We fix the hardware so it functions the way it was meant to.

### New exit devices and storefront exits

We install rim exit devices and mortise exit devices on storefronts, back doors and stairwell doors, with outside trim where the door needs to be opened from outside with a key, and we set the closer so the door latches on its own. Aluminum storefront doors take specific devices and mounting, which is covered on the storefront door hardware page. Where an opening has to be secured tonight and the permanent hardware is days away, we can fit temporary lockup hardware and come back for it at the install.

### Questions and answers

**My panic bar won't latch on a fire exit. Is that urgent?** Yes. An exit device that does not latch leaves the opening unsecured, and on a fire-rated door it is a life safety issue, not a convenience issue. Send a photo of the device and the strike and we will tell you what it takes.

**What is the difference between a rim exit device and a mortise exit device?** A rim device mounts on the surface of the door and latches into a strike on the frame; it is the common choice on single doors and storefronts. A mortise device has a lock body set into the edge of the door, with the bar operating it, and is used on heavier doors and where a mortise pocket already exists. Vertical rod devices latch at the top and bottom of the door instead, which is how pairs of doors without a center post are secured.

**Can you fix the hardware on a fire exit door?** Yes. We repair and replace closers, exit devices, latches and locks on fire exit doors so the door closes on its own, latches every time and opens freely from the inside, using hardware rated for a fire door. We do not inspect or certify fire door assemblies, and we do not replace doors or frames.

**Can a panic bar be locked from the outside?** The bar itself always opens from the inside with one push; that is the point of it. What controls the outside is the trim: a lever or pull with a cylinder that can be locked or left unlocked. We install and rekey exit device trim so the outside behaves the way you need while the inside stays free.

**Why does my exit door not close all the way?** Usually the closer, not the exit device. A closer with its latch speed set too slow or its spring set too light leaves the door resting on the latch, and air pressure from the building's air conditioning can hold an exterior door open. We set or replace the closer and check the hinges, strike and alignment so the door seats and latches on its own.


## Door closer repair, adjustment and replacement in Tampa

URL: https://prioritylocks.com/door-closers

A door that slams, a door that never quite latches, a door that takes two hands to open: the closer is usually the reason, and Tampa heat and humidity are hard on closers. Priority Lock and Security adjusts, repairs and replaces door closers on commercial doors across Tampa, matched to the door's size, weight and traffic.

### Why does my door slam?

A door slams when the closer has lost control of its closing speed. A closer is a spring that shuts the door and a sealed hydraulic cylinder that slows it down. Two valves set the speed: one for the main swing and one for the last few inches before the latch. If a valve has been opened too far, the door slams and the valve can be reset. If the closer has leaked its fluid, no adjustment will bring it back and the closer needs to be replaced. Tampa heat thins the fluid in closers on sun-facing doors, and wind or air pressure from the air conditioning can push an exterior door shut hard. A slamming door is hard on the frame, the glass, the hinges and the lock, so it is worth fixing before it breaks something else.

### Why won't my door close and latch on its own?

Usually something is resisting the door in the last few inches, or the closer does not have enough force left to finish the job. The common causes are a closer with its latch speed set too slow or its spring set too light, a latch that is hitting the strike plate instead of dropping into it, sagging hinges or worn pivots that let the door rub the frame, new weatherstripping that is too tight, and air pressure inside the building holding the door open. We check the door first and the closer second, because a stronger closer on a door that is binding only hides the problem and makes the door harder to open. A door that does not latch is an unlocked door, even when the lock is locked.

### Oil on the closer or running down the door

That closer has to be replaced. The oil is the hydraulic fluid that controls the door's speed; once a seal has failed, the door will close faster and faster until it slams, and adjusting the valves will not help for long. When we replace a closer we match it to the door: the size and weight of the door, interior or exterior, how the old closer was mounted, and how much traffic it sees. Sizing matters. A closer that is too light will not latch the door, and one that is too heavy makes the door hard to open. We clean up the oil too, because it stains the door and makes the floor slick.

### Why is my door so hard to open?

Most often the closer spring is set stronger than the door needs, or the door itself is binding. Somebody may have turned the spring power up to force a door to latch, which treats the symptom and makes the door heavy for everyone. Other causes are a backcheck setting that starts resisting too early in the swing, hinges or pivots that are worn or dry, a door rubbing the frame or the threshold, and air pressure working against the door. Accessibility rules also limit how much force a door can take to open, so a heavy door is more than an annoyance. We find what is fighting the door, fix that, then set the closer to the lightest setting that still closes and latches the door reliably.

### Concealed and storefront closers

Aluminum storefront doors often hide the closer in the frame above the door or in the floor. Those closers wear the same way and are replaced with the same care about size and mounting, alongside the pivots that carry the door. See the storefront door hardware page.

### Questions and answers

**Can a slamming door be adjusted, or does the closer need to be replaced?** Most slamming doors can be adjusted: the closer's speed valves are reset and the spring is checked. A closer that is leaking oil has to be replaced, because once the seals are gone it cannot be refilled and will slam again within days.

**How much force should a commercial door take to open?** Accessibility rules limit the force on interior doors to about five pounds, and exterior doors are expected to open with reasonable force as well. A door that takes a shoulder to open usually has a closer set too strong or a door that is binding, and both are fixable.

**Why does my door close fine in the morning and slam in the afternoon?** Heat. The hydraulic fluid in a closer thins as the door warms in the sun, so a closer that is marginal in the morning loses control by afternoon. A closer in good condition can be set to hold across that range; one that is worn or leaking cannot.

**Do you replace closers on fire exit doors?** Yes. A fire door has to close and latch on its own every time, so a failed closer on one is a life safety problem. We replace it with a closer rated for the door and set the latch speed so the door seats. See the panic bar and exit device page for the rest of the fire exit hardware.


## Aluminum storefront door hardware repair in Tampa

URL: https://prioritylocks.com/storefront-doors

Glass storefront doors sag, drag and stop locking as their pivots wear. Priority Lock and Security repairs the hardware on aluminum and glass storefront doors across Tampa: hook bolt and deadlatch locks, key cylinders, pivots, concealed closers, exit devices and door alignment. We repair the hardware; we do not replace doors or frames.

### Why won't my glass storefront door lock?

On an aluminum and glass storefront door, the usual cause is that the door has sagged and the bolt no longer lines up with its opening in the frame or the other door. Most of these doors use a narrow lock in the door's edge with a hook shaped or swinging bolt that pivots out when you turn the key. When the pivots or hinges wear, the door drops a fraction of an inch and the bolt hits metal. On a pair of doors, the bolt locks into the second door, so that door's top and bottom bolts have to be engaged or the pair will pull open even when locked. Less often, the lock body itself has broken inside. The fix starts with getting the door hanging correctly again, then the lock.

### The key cylinder is loose or spins

Fix it soon. The cylinder on a storefront door threads into the lock body and is held by a small set screw in the edge of the door. When that screw backs out, the cylinder loosens, turns with the key and stops operating the bolt. You can end up with a door that will not lock, or one that will not unlock. It is also a security problem, because a loose cylinder can be twisted out of the door by hand. The repair resets the cylinder to the right depth so its cam lines up with the lock, secures the set screw, and checks that the trim ring around the cylinder is tight and not easy to grip with a tool.

### The door drags on the threshold or rubs the frame

The door has dropped, and on a storefront door that almost always means worn or loose pivots. Most aluminum glass doors hang on a top pivot and a bottom pivot, sometimes with one in between, instead of hinges. The bottom pivot carries the weight of the door, and with years of traffic it wears, loosens, or its screws pull out of the thin aluminum. The door sags toward the latch side, scrapes the threshold, rubs the frame at the top corner and the lock stops lining up. We adjust or replace the pivots, check the closer, which is often hidden in the frame above the door, and reset the door so it swings clear and locks.

### Push bars, pulls and exit devices on storefronts

Storefront exits use rim exit devices or concealed vertical rod devices mounted to the narrow aluminum stile, and those take specific hardware and mounting. We repair and replace them, along with the push and pull handles, the deadlatches on the exit side and the outside cylinders. See panic bars and exit devices .

### Rekeying storefront cylinders

Storefront locks use a mortise cylinder that threads out of the door, which makes them quick to rekey when a manager or an employee leaves, and easy to bring into a master key system with the rest of the building. Keys are cut on site.

### Questions and answers

**Can you fix a storefront door without replacing it?** In most cases, yes. The door itself is usually fine; the pivots, the lock, the cylinder or the closer have worn. We replace the worn hardware and reset the door. We do not replace doors or frames, and if a door is past saving we will say so.

**What kind of lock is on a glass storefront door?** Most aluminum storefront doors use a narrow stile deadlock with a hook bolt or a swing bolt, operated by a mortise cylinder on the outside and a thumbturn or a second cylinder inside, plus a deadlatch under the push and pull handles on many exits. A photo of the edge of the door tells us which one you have.

**My double doors pull open even when locked. Why?** On a pair of doors, the lock in the active door bolts into the inactive door, and the inactive door is held only by its own top and bottom flush bolts. If those are not engaged, or their strikes are worn, the pair pulls open. We repair the flush bolts and strikes and realign the pair.

**Do you work on the closers hidden in storefront door frames?** Yes. Concealed overhead closers and floor closers wear the same way as surface closers, and a failing one lets the door slam or leaves it unlatched. We adjust or replace them along with the pivots that carry the door.


## Rekeying and lock changes for Tampa businesses

URL: https://prioritylocks.com/rekeying

When keys go missing, staff leave, or a building changes hands, the old keys have to stop working. Priority Lock and Security rekeys commercial locks on site across Tampa, changes out worn hardware, keys new locks to your existing system, and cuts the keys you need, counted and recorded.

### Rekey or replace?

Rekeying means we take the lock cylinder apart and change the pins inside so it works with a new key and the old keys no longer turn. The lock, the lever and the door stay. It is the right call after staff changes, lost keys, a tenant turnover, or buying a building with an unknown key history, as long as the hardware is in good condition. Replacing the lock makes sense when the hardware is worn out, is the wrong grade for the door, or a different kind of lock is needed. We look at the hardware before recommending either one. Many commercial buildings need some of each: most locks rekeyed, a few worn ones replaced.

### An employee left and did not return the keys

Rekey the locks those keys operated. There is no way to know whether a key was copied, so getting a key back does not fully settle it either. Start with a list of which doors that person's key opened. If it was one or two doors, those cylinders get rekeyed and new keys go to the people who need them. If the person carried a master key, the exposure is wider and every lock under that master is affected, which takes a plan and can be done in stages so the building keeps running.

### Buying or taking over a building

You cannot know how many copies of the old keys exist, and a rekey makes every one of them useless for far less than replacing hardware. The standard recommendation when you take over a building is to rekey it to a written plan: which doors group together, who gets which key, and one master for you. That plan is a master key system , and it is designed on paper first so it has room to grow.

### Keyed alike, and keys cut for your system

Most of the doors in a business can work on one key, as long as the locks share a keyway or can be fitted with cylinders that do. Before doing it, think about who should open what: one key for everything is convenient for an owner and a problem if the same key is handed to every employee. We cut keys for the buildings we service, to the codes on file, so copies come from one place and get counted.

### Mailbox locks

For apartment and office buildings we replace and rekey the tenant compartment locks on privately owned cluster mailboxes at turnover or when keys are lost. The carrier's master lock on the panel belongs to the Postal Service, and only they can service it.

### What you get

Rekeyed on site, usually in one visit, with new keys issued in a counted set and the date, the door and the number of keys recorded. Residential rekeys are on the residential locksmith page.

### Questions and answers

**What is the difference between rekeying and replacing a lock?** Rekeying changes the pins inside the lock so the old keys stop working and the hardware stays. Replacing swaps the lock itself, for worn or damaged hardware or an upgrade. Rekeying is cheaper and is usually the right answer when the hardware is sound.

**Should I rekey when a tenant moves out or when I take over a building?** Yes, and it is the standard recommendation. You cannot know how many copies of the old keys exist, and a rekey makes every one of them useless for far less than replacing hardware. In a master keyed building the rekey should go through the locksmith who keeps the building's key records, so the suite stays on the master.

**Can all the doors in my business work on one key?** Usually yes. Keying locks alike means pinning every cylinder to the same key, and it works as long as the locks share a keyway or can be fitted with cylinders that do. Where a building has a mix of lock brands, some cylinders may need to be swapped. Often the better setup is a small master key system: staff keys that open only the doors each person needs, and one key for the owner that opens everything.

**Does stamping Do Not Duplicate on a key stop it from being copied?** No. The stamp is a request, not a control. If the key blank is sold on the open market, anyone with a key machine or a self service kiosk can copy it. Real key control comes from a written key plan with counted keys, and from a restricted keyway where the blanks are not sold openly. Ask before your next rekey; that is the cheapest time to change how your keys are controlled.

**How long does a rekey take?** A few cylinders are done in under an hour on site, keys included. A whole floor or building is planned and can be done in stages so nobody is locked out during the day.


## Tenant turnover lock changes in Tampa

URL: https://prioritylocks.com/tenant-turnover

When a tenant moves out, the suite should be rekeyed before the next tenant gets keys, and the work should go through the building's locksmith so the suite stays on your master key. Priority Lock and Security handles turnover rekeys for apartment communities, office buildings and mixed-use properties across Tampa, usually the same week.

### What should happen to the locks when a tenant moves out?

The suite gets rekeyed, not just the keys collected. You cannot know how many copies the outgoing tenant made, and a rekey makes every one of them useless for far less than new hardware. Rekeying changes the pins inside the existing locks so the old keys stop working; the levers and deadbolts stay on the door. We rekey the entry, any interior locks the tenant controlled, and the mailbox compartment if the building has private cluster boxes, then issue a counted set of new keys and record the date, the door and the number of keys.

### Why the building's locksmith should do it, not the tenant's

In a master keyed building, every suite lock is pinned to work with both its own key and the building master. When an outgoing or incoming tenant hires their own locksmith, that suite usually falls off the master key, and nobody finds out until maintenance or the fire department needs to get in. Handling every turnover through one vendor keeps the master working, keeps the key records accurate, and gives you a dated record of when the suite was rekeyed and how many keys were issued. The lease decides who pays; who does the work matters more than most people expect.

### What a turnover visit covers

  - Entry lock and deadbolt rekeyed to a new change key, kept on the building master.

  - Interior locks the tenant controlled, and the mailbox lock, on the same visit.

  - Worn hardware flagged, and replaced if you want it done while we are there: a drooping lever, a deadbolt that stops short, a closer that slams.

  - A counted key set and a record of what was done, for your file and the new tenant's.

### Buildings with no key records

Most managers inherit a building with no key records, a ring of unlabeled keys, and a few suites somebody else rekeyed years ago. The fix is a door and key survey and a rekey to a written plan, done in stages if needed. That is a master key system , and once it exists every later turnover fits the same plan.

### Questions and answers

**How fast can a turnover be rekeyed?** Usually within the week, and often sooner. Text the building, the suite and the move out date to 813-421-4787 and we schedule it so the suite is ready before the new tenant's keys are handed over.

**Do you rekey apartments as well as offices?** Yes. Apartment communities, office suites, retail bays and mixed-use buildings. The work is the same: rekey the suite inside the building's key system, count the keys, record it.

**Who pays for a turnover rekey?** The lease decides. Many leases make the outgoing tenant responsible for keys not returned and the owner responsible for rekeying between tenants. Whatever the lease says about money, the work itself should go through the building's locksmith so the suite stays on the master key.

**Can the new tenant keep the old keys instead?** They can, but then every copy the previous tenant ever made still opens the door. A rekey is the only way to know the new tenant holds the only keys.


## Master key systems and key control in Tampa

URL: https://prioritylocks.com/master-key-systems

A master key system gives every tenant a key that opens only their own door and gives you one key that opens everything, with a written record of who holds what. Priority Lock and Security designs, installs and maintains master key systems for multi-tenant buildings, office complexes and apartment communities across Tampa.

### What a master key system is

A master key system is a planned set of locks where each door has its own key and a master key opens all of them. Each tenant or department key opens only its own door. The master opens every door in the group, and larger properties add levels: a master for each floor or building and a grand master above those. The system is designed on paper first, as a keying schedule, so it has room to grow without repinning the whole building later. The records are what make it work over time, and we keep those records for the buildings we service.

### Does my building need one?

Probably, if you have multiple tenants or departments, if maintenance and management carry a ring of keys, or if you need reliable entry to every space in an emergency. A building running on keyed alike locks and a drawer of spares works until the first lost key, and then every door has to be treated as exposed. A master key system turns that into a smaller job: rekey the one door, issue one key, update the record.

### Getting control of a building with no key records

Start with a survey of the doors and an honest list of who holds keys today. We walk the building, record each door with its hardware and keyway, test which existing keys open what, and note anything worn or not latching. From that we lay out a keying plan: which doors group together, who needs which level of key, and whether to stay on the current keyway or move to one that is harder to copy. Then the building is rekeyed to the new plan, in stages if needed, with keys issued against a signed record. This situation is normal, especially in older multi-tenant buildings in Ybor City and downtown Tampa that have passed through several owners and managers. It is fixable, and once fixed it stays fixed if the records are kept.

### We lost the master key

Treat every lock under that master as exposed and plan a rekey of the system. A lost master is different from a lost suite key, because it opens every door in its group. The work can be staged: exterior doors and sensitive rooms first, then the rest, so the building keeps operating while the change is made. Tenant keys change too, because each lock is pinned to both its own key and the master, so tenants need notice and new keys.

### Key control

Key control is the habit that keeps a master key system honest: every key that goes out is written down, keys come back at turnover, copies come from one place, and the records are kept current. Stamping Do Not Duplicate on a key is a request, not a control; if the blank is sold openly, anyone with a key machine can copy it. Where copies have to be impossible without you, the answer is a restricted keyway, where blanks are not sold on the open market. Ask before the next rekey; that is the cheapest time to change keyways.

### Questions and answers

**What is a master key system, and does my building need one?** A master key system is a planned set of locks where each door has its own key and a master key opens all of them. Your building likely needs one if you have multiple tenants or departments, if maintenance and management carry a ring of keys, or if you need reliable entry to every space in an emergency. It is designed on paper first so it has room to grow.

**How do I keep control of who has keys?** A master key system with a key log: tenants get their own key, you keep one that opens everything, and every key that goes out is written down and comes back at turnover. For copies to be impossible without you, the building moves to a restricted keyway, which is easiest to do at a rekey.

**Can a master key system be added to my existing locks?** Often, yes. If the existing locks share a keyway, or can be fitted with cylinders that do, they are repinned to the new keying schedule without changing the hardware on the doors. Worn locks are replaced in the same pass.

**What happens when a tenant moves out of a master keyed building?** The suite is rekeyed to a new change key and stays on the master, new keys are issued in a counted set, and the record is updated. If the tenant's own locksmith rekeys it instead, the suite usually drops off the master and nobody finds out until somebody needs to get in.

**What is a restricted key?** A restricted key is a key that cannot be copied at a hardware store, a kiosk or another locksmith shop, because the blanks are not sold on the open market and copies are cut only for people the owner has authorized in writing. It is the practical foundation of key control for multi-tenant and commercial buildings, and it can be built into a master key system.

### Door closers

**Why does my door slam?** A door slams when the door closer has lost control of its closing speed. A closer is a spring that shuts the door and a sealed hydraulic cylinder that slows it down. Two valves set the speed: one for the main swing and one for the last few inches before the latch. If a valve has been opened too far, the door slams and the valve can be reset. If the closer has leaked its fluid, no adjustment will bring it back and the closer needs to be replaced. Wind and air pressure from the building's air conditioning can also push a door shut hard, which is common on exterior doors in Tampa. A slamming door is hard on the frame, the glass, the hinges and the lock, so it is worth fixing before it breaks something else.

**Why won't my door close and latch all the way on its own?** Usually something is resisting the door in the last few inches, or the closer does not have enough force left to finish the job. The common causes are a closer with its latch speed set too slow or its spring set too light, a latch that is hitting the strike plate instead of dropping into it, sagging hinges or worn pivots that let the door rub the frame, new weatherstripping that is too tight, and air pressure inside the building holding the door open. We check the door first and the closer second, because a stronger closer on a door that is binding only hides the problem and makes the door harder to open. A door that does not latch is an unlocked door, even when the lock is locked.

**There is oil on my door closer or dripping down the door. Can it be fixed?** No. A closer that is leaking oil has a failed seal, and it has to be replaced. The oil is the hydraulic fluid that controls the door's speed. Once it is leaking out, the door will close faster and faster until it slams, and adjusting the valves will not help for long. When we replace a closer we match it to the door: the size and weight of the door, whether it is an interior or exterior opening, how the old closer was mounted, and how much traffic the door sees. A closer that is too light for the door will not latch it, and one that is too heavy makes the door hard to open. We also clean up the oil, because it stains the door and makes the floor slick.

**Why is my door so hard to open?** Most often the closer spring is set stronger than the door needs, or the door itself is binding. Someone may have turned the spring power up to force a door to latch, which treats the symptom and makes the door heavy for everyone who uses it. Other causes are a backcheck setting that starts resisting too early in the swing, hinges or pivots that are worn or dry, a door rubbing the frame or the threshold, and air pressure in the building working against the door. Accessibility rules also limit how much force a door can take to open, so a heavy door is more than an annoyance. We find what is actually fighting the door, fix that, and then set the closer to the lightest setting that still closes and latches the door reliably.


### Exit devices and panic bars

**Why won't my panic bar latch?** A panic bar that will not latch is almost always a door alignment problem, a strike problem, or a bar that has been left dogged. If the door has sagged, the latch hits the strike instead of landing behind it. If the strike on the frame is loose or has shifted, the latch has nothing solid to catch. If the bar has been dogged, held in the pushed-in position with a hex key or a cylinder, the latch stays pulled back on purpose and the door swings freely. On doors with vertical rods, a rod that is out of adjustment will keep the top or bottom latch from catching. A weak or slow door closer can also leave the door resting against the latch without ever seating it. We check all of these in order, because more than one is often involved.

**Why does my panic bar stick, drag, or not pull the latch back all the way?** A bar that sticks or does not fully retract the latch usually has worn or broken parts inside, loose mounting, or a door that is pressing against the latch. Exit devices take a lot of abuse: carts, shoulders, kicks, and years of daily traffic. Springs break, internal linkages wear, end caps get knocked loose, and mounting screws back out so the whole device shifts on the door. On vertical rod devices, bent or misadjusted rods drag and bind. Sometimes the device is fine and the door is warped or out of alignment, which puts pressure on the latch so the bar has to be hit hard to release it. An exit device is life safety hardware. It has to open with one push every time, so a sticking bar should be repaired or replaced, not lived with.

**What is dogging, and how do I keep a panic bar door unlocked during business hours?** Dogging is the feature that holds the panic bar in and the latch pulled back, so the door works as a push and pull door during business hours. On most devices you push the bar in and turn a hex key (or a regular key, on cylinder dogging models) to hold it. Undo it at closing time and the door latches and locks again. If a door keeps turning up unlocked in the morning, check whether someone left it dogged. One important exception: exit devices on fire-rated doors do not have mechanical dogging, because a fire door has to latch every time it closes. If you need that kind of door unlocked during the day, the outside lever or trim is what gets unlocked, and the latch still catches. We can tell you which type you have.

**Can you repair the hardware on a fire exit door?** Yes. We repair and replace the closers, exit devices, latches and locks on fire exit doors so the door closes on its own, latches every time, and opens freely from the inside. Those are the basic things that hardware has to do, and they are the things that usually fail: a closer that no longer shuts the door, a latch that does not catch, a bar that sticks, or a door that someone has propped or wedged open. Replacement hardware on a fire-rated door has to be rated for that use, and we select it accordingly. To be clear about what we do not do: we do not inspect or certify fire door assemblies, and we do not replace doors or frames. We fix the hardware so it functions the way it was meant to.


### Locks and levers

**What is the difference between grade 1 and grade 2 hardware?** Grade 1 is the heaviest duty commercial rating and grade 2 is a step below it, built for lighter commercial use. The grades come from ANSI/BHMA standards, which test locks for how many open and close cycles they survive, how much force and abuse they take, and how the finish holds up. Grade 1 belongs on doors that see heavy traffic or rough treatment: main entries, common area doors, public restrooms, stairwells, back doors that get hit with carts. Grade 2 is a sound choice for office suite entries and interior doors with normal traffic. Grade 3 is residential hardware and does not belong on a commercial door. Most of the failed levers we see on busy doors are the wrong grade for the door they were put on, not defective locks.

**Why is my door lever loose, drooping, or wobbly?** A loose lever usually means the mounting screws that clamp the lock through the door have backed out. A drooping lever means the spring that holds the lever level has worn out or broken. On a commercial lever lock, the two sides are bolted to each other through the door, and daily use works those bolts loose over time. Caught early, the lock can be taken apart, checked, and properly tightened. Left alone, the lock shifts in the door, the latch stops lining up, internal parts wear, and eventually the lever spins free or comes off in someone's hand. A sagging lever is a worn return spring, often in a light duty lock on a busy door. In that case replacement with the correct grade of lock is usually the better repair.

**What is a mortise lock, and can it be repaired?** A mortise lock is a heavy lock body that sits in a pocket cut into the edge of the door, with the lever, the cylinder and often a deadbolt all working through that one case. Yes, most can be repaired. Mortise locks are built to be serviced: the case can be opened, cleaned, and rebuilt with new springs and parts, and the key cylinder threads in and out separately, so rekeying does not disturb the lock body. They are common in older commercial buildings, which Ybor City and downtown Tampa have plenty of. The catch is that the pocket in the door is cut for a specific size of lock body. When a mortise lock is past repair, the replacement has to match that pocket and the existing trim holes, so identifying the lock correctly matters before any parts are ordered.

**Why is my key hard to turn, or why does it stick in the lock?** The usual causes are a worn key, a worn or dirty cylinder, or a bolt that is binding against the frame. Here is a useful test: open the door and try the key with the door open. If it turns freely, the lock is fine and the door is out of alignment, so the bolt or latch is rubbing the strike. If it is still stiff with the door open, the problem is in the key or the cylinder. Keys that are copies of copies drift out of spec, and a fresh key cut from the original code often fixes it. Cylinders also wear and collect grit, especially on exterior doors. Avoid spraying oil into the keyway, because it holds dirt and makes things worse over time. A key that is getting harder to turn is a key that will eventually break off in the lock.

**Is my deadbolt actually locked?** Only if the bolt is thrown all the way out. A bolt that stops halfway into the frame has almost nothing holding it and can be forced. If your key stops short or grinds, or you have to pull the door toward you to turn it, the frame or the strike needs correcting. That is a quick fix and it is the difference between a locked door and a door that looks locked.

**Do you work on mailbox locks?** Yes, for apartment and office buildings. We replace and rekey the tenant compartment locks on privately owned cluster mailboxes at turnover or when keys are lost. The carrier's master lock on the panel belongs to the Postal Service, and only they can service it.


### Storefront doors (aluminum and glass)

**Why won't my glass storefront door lock?** On an aluminum and glass storefront door, the usual cause is that the door has sagged and the bolt no longer lines up with its opening in the frame or the other door. Most of these doors use a narrow lock in the door's edge with a hook shaped or swinging bolt that pivots out when you turn the key. When the pivots or hinges wear, the door drops a fraction of an inch and the bolt hits metal. On a pair of doors, the bolt locks into the second door, so that door's top and bottom bolts have to be engaged or the pair will pull open even when locked. Less often, the lock body itself has broken inside. It is a common problem on busy storefronts in Tampa, and the fix starts with getting the door hanging correctly again.

**The key cylinder on my storefront door is loose or spins. Is that a problem?** Yes, and it should be fixed soon. The key cylinder on a storefront door threads into the lock body and is held in place by a small set screw in the edge of the door. When that screw backs out, the cylinder loosens, turns with the key, and stops operating the bolt. You can end up with a door that will not lock, or one that will not unlock. It is also a security problem, because a loose cylinder can be twisted out of the door by hand. The repair involves resetting the cylinder to the right depth so its cam lines up with the lock, securing the set screw, and checking that the trim ring around the cylinder is tight and not easy to grip with a tool.

**Why does my storefront door drag on the threshold or rub the frame?** The door has dropped, and on a storefront door that almost always means worn or loose pivots. Most aluminum glass doors hang on a top pivot and a bottom pivot, sometimes with one in between, instead of regular hinges. The bottom pivot carries the weight of the door, and with years of traffic it wears, loosens, or its screws pull out of the thin aluminum. The door then sags toward the latch side, scrapes the threshold, rubs the frame at the top corner, and the lock stops lining up. We adjust or replace the pivots, check the closer (which is often hidden in the frame above the door), and reset the door so it swings clear and locks. We repair the hardware. We do not replace doors or frames.


### Keys and rekeying

**Can you rekey instead of replacing locks?** Yes, and when the hardware is in good condition, rekeying is usually the right call. Rekeying means we take the lock cylinder apart and change the pins inside so it works with a new key and the old keys no longer turn. The lock, the lever and the door are untouched. It makes sense after tenant turnover, staff changes, lost keys, or buying a building with an unknown key history. Replacing the lock makes sense when the hardware is worn out, is the wrong grade for the door, or a different kind of lock is needed. We look at the hardware before recommending either one. Many commercial buildings in Tampa need some of each: most locks rekeyed, a few worn ones replaced.

**Who should rekey a building after a tenant moves out?** The property manager or owner should control it, using the locksmith who keeps the building's key records. The lease decides who pays, but who does the work matters more than most people expect. In a master keyed building, every suite lock is pinned to work with both its own key and the building master. If an outgoing or incoming tenant hires their own locksmith, that suite usually falls off the master key, and nobody finds out until maintenance or the fire department needs to get in. Handling every turnover rekey through one vendor keeps the master working, keeps the key records accurate, and gives you a dated record of when the suite was rekeyed and how many keys were issued. For property managers in Tampa and Ybor City, tenant turnover rekeys are routine work for us.

**An employee left and did not return their keys. What should I do?** Rekey the locks those keys operated. There is no way to know whether a key was copied, so getting a key back does not fully settle it either. Start with a list of which doors that person's key opened. If it was one or two doors, those cylinders get rekeyed and new keys go to the people who need them. If the person carried a master key, the exposure is wider and the plan needs more thought, because every lock under that master is affected. After that, a departing employee means collecting a key you know is the only one, because copies come from one place and are written down.

**Can all the doors in my business work on one key?** Usually yes. Keying locks alike means pinning every cylinder to the same key, and it works as long as the locks share the same keyway (the shape of the key slot) or can be fitted with cylinders that do. Where a building has a mix of lock brands, some cylinders may need to be swapped so everything accepts one key. Before doing it, think about who should open what. One key for everything is convenient for an owner and a problem if the same key is handed to every employee. Often the better setup is a small master key system: staff keys that open only the doors each person needs, and one key for the owner or manager that opens everything.

**Do you cut keys?** Yes, for the buildings and homes we service: keys cut to the codes on file for your key system, so copies come from one place and get counted. We are not a walk-in key shop, and we do not cut car keys.


### Master keys and key control

**What is a master key system, and does my building need one?** A master key system is a planned set of locks where each door has its own key, and a master key opens all of them. Each tenant or department key opens only its own door. The master opens every door in the group, and larger properties can add levels, such as a master for each floor or building and a grand master above those. Your building likely needs one if you have multiple tenants or departments, if maintenance and management carry a ring of keys, or if you need reliable entry to every space in an emergency. The system is designed on paper first, as a keying schedule, so it has room to grow. The records are what make it work over time, and we maintain those records for buildings we service in Tampa.

**What is a restricted key?** A restricted key is a key that cannot be copied at a hardware store, a kiosk, or another locksmith shop, because the key blanks are not sold on the open market. The keyway is protected by a manufacturer's patent or by contract, and blanks are supplied only to authorized dealers. Copies are cut only for people the owner has authorized in writing, and each key is tracked. The result is that you know exactly how many keys exist for your building and who holds them. For a property manager, that changes turnover: when every key issued comes back, you know the suite is secure. Restricted keys are the practical foundation of key control for multi-tenant and commercial buildings, and they can be built into a master key system.

**What is the difference between a restricted key and a high security lock?** Restricted refers to who can copy the key. High security refers to how well the lock resists attack. A restricted key system controls key blanks so keys cannot be duplicated without authorization. A high security lock adds physical protection: resistance to picking, drilling and other forced methods, often tested to a published standard such as UL 437. Many high security cylinders also come with restricted keys, so you get both. If your concern is unknown copies of keys floating around among former tenants and employees, restricted keys address it. If the concern is a determined break-in through the lock itself on an exterior door or a room with valuable contents, high security cylinders are worth discussing.

**Does stamping Do Not Duplicate on a key stop it from being copied?** No. The stamp is a request, not a control. If the key blank is sold on the open market, anyone with a key machine or a self service kiosk can copy it, and many will without looking at what is stamped on it. Real key control comes from a written key plan with counted keys, and from a restricted keyway where blanks are available only to authorized dealers. If you manage a building and your plan for controlling keys depends on the words stamped on them, assume there are more copies out there than your records show. The practical fix is to move to a restricted key at the next rekey, so the cost and disruption are folded into work you were already going to do.

**Nobody knows who has keys to our building. Where do we start?** Start with a survey of the doors and an honest list of who holds keys today. We walk the building, record each door and what hardware and keyway it has, test which existing keys open what, and note anything that is worn or not latching. From that we lay out a keying plan: which doors group together, who needs which level of key, and whether to stay on the current keyway or move to a restricted one. Then the building is rekeyed to the new plan, in stages if needed, with keys issued against a signed record. This situation is normal, especially in older multi-tenant buildings in Ybor City and downtown Tampa that have passed through several owners and managers. It is fixable, and once fixed it stays fixed if the records are kept.

**We lost the master key. What now?** Treat every lock under that master as exposed, and plan a rekey of the system. A lost master is different from a lost suite key, because it opens every door in its group. If the key could be tied to your building (it was on a labeled ring, or lost on site), act sooner. The work can be staged: exterior doors and sensitive rooms first, then the rest, so the building keeps operating while the change is made. Tenant keys also change, because each lock is pinned to both its own key and the master, so tenants need notice and new keys. If your building is still on a key that can be copied anywhere, this is the right time to move to a restricted keyway.


### Homes

**Do you rekey houses?** Yes. New house, lost keys, a roommate or a contractor who still has a key: we rekey every exterior door to one new key on site, replace worn locks and deadbolts, and cut the copies you need. See the residential locksmith page. We do not do car keys or safes.

**Should I rekey or replace the locks on a new house?** Rekey, if the locks are in good condition: the old keys stop working and the hardware stays. Replace a lock only when it is worn, loose or the wrong kind for the door. Many houses need a rekey on most doors and a new deadbolt on one.

**Do you do house lockouts?** We are a scheduled service company rather than an emergency lockout line, so during business hours text 813-421-4787 and we will tell you plainly what we can do and when. We do not do car lockouts.
